taxonomyNote: NatureServe's standard name is 'Eastern Musk Turtle'; 'Stinkpot' and 'Common Musk Turtle' are alternates.
fieldMarks: Small turtle, adults 100-127 mm; narrow, elongated brown domed carapace with black streaks or spots, often algae-covered.
Two light (pale yellow) stripes on each side of the head, one above and one below the eye, distinguish it from other Sternotherus.
Elongated pointed snout with barbels on the chin and neck; small yellow plastron with a single non-functional hinge and skin showing between the plastral scutes.
Males have larger heads and longer tails than females.
behavior: Mostly aquatic and crepuscular (more nocturnal in the south); bottom walker that basks on branches up to 2 m above the water and may drop into passing boats.
Brumates buried about 30 cm in mud when water is below about 10 C; active April-October in the north.
Threatened animals release a foul-smelling orange musk from glands under the shell.
Omnivorous: algae, seeds, insects, mollusks, crayfish, carrion and fish.
habitat: Virtually any permanent freshwater with slow current and soft bottom and plenty of aquatic plants: ponds, lakes, impoundments, streams, rivers and swamps.
range: Eastern and central United States from southern Maine, Michigan and Wisconsin to Florida and east Texas (absent from higher elevations); in Canada southern Ontario and Quebec (NatureServe rank N3; federally Special Concern).

lookalikes.name: Striped mud turtle
lookalikes.howToTell: Mud turtles have two plastral hinges and unkeeled carapaces, and lack skin visible between plastral scutes (Animal Diversity Web).

lookalikes.name: Eastern mud turtle
lookalikes.howToTell: Two hinges on the plastron and a never-keeled carapace; stinkpots show skin between plastron scutes (Animal Diversity Web).
